tips.title: Two words, two jobs
tips.body: **Decomposition** breaks a problem **into parts**. **Abstraction** removes **unnecessary detail**. One splits, the other strips. Mixing them up is the commonest error on this part of the specification, and the two words are worth learning as a pair.

tips.title: Each sub-problem must name a task
tips.body: The specification says each sub-problem should accomplish an **identifiable task**. So write sub-problems as **things to do** — *mark the answers* — not as topics — *marking*. If you cannot say what it does, it is not a sub-problem yet.

tips.title: "Unnecessary" depends on the purpose
tips.body: There is no list of details that are always unnecessary. A detail is unnecessary **for a particular purpose**. Walking distance is unnecessary on an Underground map and essential on a street map, so always say what the abstraction is *for*.

tips.title: Name the detail you removed
tips.body: An answer that says *abstraction removes unnecessary detail* repeats the definition. Naming a specific detail — *the real distances between stations* — and saying **why** it can go is what turns a definition into an explanation.

tips.title: Sub-problems can subdivide again
tips.body: The specification adds that a sub-problem **might itself be further subdivided**. So decomposition is not one cut into three pieces; it carries on until each part is small enough to solve directly.

why.matters:
Nobody writes a large program. They write a lot of small ones that fit together, and the two ideas in this topic are how a problem gets small enough to start on.

**Decomposition** splits it; **abstraction** strips it. They are easy to confuse because both make a problem simpler, and the exam asks you to name which is which — so the question to hold is whether the problem has been **cut into parts** or had **detail removed**.

examples.title: Why nobody starts by writing "build a quiz app"
examples.body:
That is not a thing anyone can begin. Broken into parts it is: pick the questions, ask one and read the answer, mark it, show the score — and every one of those is small enough to start today.

Each sub-problem has to accomplish an **identifiable task**, which is why they are written as verbs. And any of them can be split again: *mark it* becomes compare the answer, allow for capitals, allow for spaces. Decomposition is not one cut into pieces; it is a cut repeated until the pieces are obvious.

examples.title: Why the Underground map is the wrong shape
examples.body:
It is not a map of London. The distances are wrong, the angles are wrong and the river is roughly a suggestion — and it is far more useful than an accurate one, which is the clearest example of **abstraction** there is.

A passenger needs to know which line, which direction and where to change. Everything else is **unnecessary detail** for that purpose, and removing it leaves something readable at arm's length on a moving train. Notice the qualifier: the same details are essential to somebody digging a tunnel. A detail is unnecessary **for a particular purpose**, never in general.

examples.title: Has it been split, or stripped?
examples.body:
The exam gives you a scenario and asks which idea it shows, so the two need a test that takes a second.

**Split into parts** — decomposition. **Detail left out** — abstraction. A satnav that treats a road as a line with a length has abstracted; a satnav built as *find the roads*, *work out the times*, *choose the route*, *give the directions* has been decomposed. Most real work does both, which is why the question is about naming what happened rather than choosing a side.

steps.title: Decomposition
steps.body:
**A big problem is hard to solve. Several small ones are not.**

The specification defines it:

> **Decomposition means breaking a problem into a number of sub-problems, so that each sub-problem accomplishes an identifiable task, which might itself be further subdivided.**

Three things in that sentence are examined.

**Breaking a problem into sub-problems.** Instead of "write a quiz app", you get "ask the questions", "mark the answers", "show the result". Each is small enough to think about on its own.

**Each accomplishes an identifiable task.** A sub-problem must be something you can **say the job of**. *Mark the answers* is a task. *Marking* is a topic, and a topic is not yet a sub-problem — you cannot start work on it.

**Which might itself be further subdivided.** *Mark the answers* still splits: compare the answer with the correct one, then add to the score. Decomposition keeps going until each piece is small enough to write directly.

**Why it helps.** Small problems are easier to solve, easier to test, and can be worked on by different people at the same time. When something goes wrong, the fault is in one small part rather than somewhere in the whole thing.

steps.title: Abstraction
steps.body:
**The specification defines abstraction too:**

> **Abstraction is the process of removing unnecessary detail from a problem.**

It does **not** break the problem up. It leaves the problem whole and throws away the parts that do not matter, so that what is left is easier to work with.

**The standard example is the Underground map.** It shows which lines run where and where you can change. It does **not** show the real distances between stations, the curves of the tunnels, or where the streets are above. All of that is real, and all of it is **unnecessary for finding your route**. The map is easier to use precisely because those things are gone.

**Nothing is unnecessary on its own.** A detail is unnecessary **for a purpose**. The real distances are unnecessary for choosing which train to catch, and essential for planning where to dig a new tunnel. So an abstraction is always an abstraction **for** something, and an answer that does not say what it is for is not finished.

**In a program,** abstraction is why a quiz app stores a student's name and score but not their eye colour. The eye colour is real; it is nothing to do with the quiz.

steps.title: Telling the two apart
steps.body:
**They are easy to confuse, and the exam asks you to name which is which.**

The question to ask is simple: **has the problem been split, or has something been thrown away?**

- Split into parts → **decomposition**
- Detail removed → **abstraction**

**Worked through on one problem — a school register app:**

*Breaking it into "take the register", "store the marks", "produce a report"* is **decomposition**. The problem is now three problems. Nothing has been discarded.

*Storing each student's name and class but not their hair colour* is **abstraction**. The problem is still one problem. A detail that does not matter has gone.

**They are used together, not instead of each other.** You decompose a problem into parts, and you abstract away the detail each part does not need. Neither replaces the other, and a good answer about designing a system usually mentions both.

**In the exam,** a question naming one of them expects the other to be kept out of your answer. Saying *decomposition removes unnecessary detail* loses the mark outright, however good the rest of the sentence is.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Learn the two definitions as a pair, because the exam tests the difference.** Decomposition **breaks a problem into sub-problems**; abstraction **removes unnecessary detail**. One splits, the other strips. Swapping them is the single commonest error here, and it costs the whole mark.

**Write sub-problems as tasks.** The specification says each must accomplish an **identifiable task**. *Mark the answers* names a job; *marking* names a topic. The test is whether you could start work on it tomorrow.

**Remember that a sub-problem might itself be further subdivided.** That clause is in the definition and is often left out of answers. Decomposition is not a single cut into three; it continues until each part is small enough to solve directly.

**Always say what the abstraction is for.** No detail is unnecessary in itself. Station distances are unnecessary **for choosing a train** and essential **for digging a tunnel**. An answer that names the purpose is doing the thing the question is actually testing.

**Name the detail you removed.** *Abstraction removes unnecessary detail* repeats the definition and shows nothing. *The map leaves out the real distances, because they do not change which train you catch* explains it. In an extended answer, one named example is worth more than a paragraph of definition.

**Say that the two work together.** A real system is decomposed into parts, and each part abstracts away what it does not need. A question about designing a system is usually looking for both, and for the fact that they are not alternatives.

**Watch for abstraction that goes too far.** Removing a detail that turns out to matter gives a model that is simple and wrong — an Underground map with the changing stations left off would be beautifully simple and useless. Judging what can go is the difficult part, not the removing.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Decomposition** breaks a problem into **sub-problems**.
- Each sub-problem must accomplish an **identifiable task**.
- A sub-problem **might itself be further subdivided**.
- Write a sub-problem as a **task** — *mark the answers* — not a topic.
- Decomposing makes parts easier to **solve**, easier to **test**, and shareable between people.
- A fault then shows up in **one small part**, not somewhere in the whole thing.
- **Abstraction** removes **unnecessary detail** from a problem.
- It leaves the problem whole; it does **not** split it.
- The Underground map keeps the **lines and changes**, removes the **distances and curves**.
- No detail is unnecessary in itself — only **unnecessary for a purpose**.
- Always state the **purpose** an abstraction serves.
- **Split or strip**: split is decomposition, strip is abstraction.
- The two are used **together**, not instead of each other.
- Abstraction taken **too far** gives a model that is simple and wrong.
- Naming the detail removed is worth more than repeating the definition.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between decomposition and abstraction, using an example of each.
questions.solution:
**Decomposition** means **breaking a problem into a number of sub-problems, so that each sub-problem accomplishes an identifiable task**, and a sub-problem **might itself be further subdivided**.

For example, "build a quiz app" is too large to start on. It decomposes into three sub-problems: **ask the questions**, **mark the answers**, and **show the result**. Each names a task you could begin work on. "Mark the answers" then subdivides again, into comparing the student's answer with the correct one and adding to the score. The splitting continues until each part is small enough to write directly.

**Abstraction** is the process of **removing unnecessary detail from a problem**. It does not split the problem up; it leaves it whole and discards what does not matter.

For example, an Underground map shows which lines run where and where you can change trains, but leaves out the real distances between stations, the curves of the tunnels and the streets above. Those details are all real. They are simply **unnecessary for planning a journey**, and leaving them out is exactly what makes the map usable.

**The difference** is that decomposition **splits** and abstraction **strips**. After decomposition there are more problems than before, and nothing has been thrown away. After abstraction there is still one problem, and some of its detail has gone. Asking "has this been split, or has something been left out?" settles which technique a situation is describing.

One further point is that **unnecessary** is not a fixed property. The distance between stations is unnecessary to a passenger choosing a train, and essential to an engineer planning where to dig. An abstraction is always an abstraction **for a purpose**, and saying what that purpose is is part of explaining it.

The two techniques are used **together**, not as alternatives. A system is decomposed into parts, and within each part the detail that part does not need is abstracted away — the quiz app's marking component needs the student's answer and score, and has no use for their name or their eye colour.

questions.prompt: A team is designing an app that helps a student manage their homework. Explain how decomposition and abstraction would be used, and what could go wrong if either were done badly.
questions.solution:
**Decomposition** would break the app into sub-problems, each **accomplishing an identifiable task**: **record a piece of homework**, **show what is due**, and **mark a piece as done**. Each is something the team could start work on.

Each of those **subdivides further**. "Record a piece of homework" splits into asking for the subject, asking for the deadline, and storing the two together. "Show what is due" splits into finding the pieces that are not yet done, sorting them by deadline, and displaying the list. The splitting stops when each part is small enough to write directly.

The benefit is practical. Each small part can be written and **tested on its own**, different members of the team can work at the same time, and when the list comes out in the wrong order the fault is in the sorting step rather than somewhere in the whole app.

**Abstraction** would then remove the detail the app does not need. For each piece of homework it would store the **subject**, the **deadline** and whether it is **done**. It would not store the teacher's room number, the colour of the exercise book, or how long the student expects the work to take — all real, none of which affects what the app must do. The reason each can go is that nothing the app does depends on it.

**If the decomposition were done badly**, the parts would not name tasks. Splitting the app into "input", "processing" and "output" looks like a decomposition, but those are the stages of **any** program: they say nothing about homework, and no one could start work from them. Parts that overlap cause a different problem — if two sub-problems both decide what counts as "due", the two can disagree, and a bug appears that is not inside either part.

**If the abstraction were done badly**, a detail that mattered would be thrown away. Storing the deadline as a **date only**, with no time, seems a harmless simplification until a piece is due at 9am and the app shows it as not yet overdue all day. The model is simpler and **wrong**. The risk runs the other way too: keeping everything — room numbers, book colours — makes the app harder to build and gives the student more to type for no benefit.

The difficult judgement in both cases is the same one. Deciding **what counts as a task** and **what counts as unnecessary** is where the design work actually is, and neither has a rule that can be applied without understanding the purpose the app is meant to serve.

examTechnique.body:
Learn both definitions in the specification's words: decomposition **breaks a problem into sub-problems, each accomplishing an identifiable task**; abstraction **removes unnecessary detail**. **Split or strip** decides which a question is describing.

Write sub-problems as **tasks**, and when explaining an abstraction, **name the detail** removed and the **purpose** that makes it unnecessary.
examinerErrors: Writing sub-problems as topics — *marking* rather than *mark the answers*.
Leaving out that a sub-problem might itself be further subdivided.
Explaining abstraction by repeating "removes unnecessary detail".
Treating "unnecessary" as fixed rather than tied to a purpose.
Decomposing into "input, processing, output", which fits any problem.
Presenting the two techniques as alternatives rather than as used together.
Assuming more abstraction is always better.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer holds the two definitions apart cleanly — **split** against **strip** — and quotes the clause that a sub-problem **might itself be further subdivided**. Its sub-problems are **tasks**, so the decomposition could be acted on. When it explains an abstraction it **names the detail** removed and the **purpose** that makes it unnecessary, rather than restating the definition. It knows the two are used **together**, and it can say what goes wrong when either is done badly: parts that name no task, or a simplification that quietly makes the model wrong.
